Graff
GRAF
verb
The older form of graft, from Old French grafe, from Latin graphium and Greek graphion, “a writing style or stylus” — so named because the cut scion is shaped like a pointed pen; hence to insert a shoot of one tree into the stock of another, that it may live by a root not its own.

Biblical Definition

To graff is the gardener’s art: to cut a living shoot and set it into the stock of another tree, that it may draw sap from a root it never grew. The KJV keeps the old spelling, and Paul makes the word carry the whole mystery of Jew and Gentile in Romans 11. The olive tree is Israel; some of the natural branches were broken off through unbelief; and the Gentile believer — a shoot of the wild olive, worthless stock, bearing nothing fit for the altar — “wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17). Mark the direction. The wild branch does not improve the tree; the tree sustains the branch. Paul presses it: thou bearest not the root, but the root thee, and “because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear.” The grafting is “contrary to nature” (Rom 11:24), for husbandmen graff the good shoot into the wild stock, never the reverse — but grace works backwards, taking what is wild and worthless and binding it into the covenant root. And the tree is one, not two: “God is able to graff them in again” (Rom 11:23), for the same door of faith stands open to the natural branches. One olive, one root, one people of God, and every branch in it — wild or natural — standing there by faith alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

To insert a shoot of one tree into the stock of another, that it may live by that root; in Romans 11, the ingrafting of the Gentiles into the olive tree.

GRAFF, the older form of graft; to insert a scion or shoot into a stock.

From Latin graphium, “a stylus,” the cut shoot resembling a pointed pen.

The graffed branch lives not by its own root but by the stock that bears it.

The wild olive was graffed in and partakes of the root and fatness (Rom 11:17).

The grafting is contrary to nature, for grace takes the wild and makes it fruitful (Rom 11:24).

Key Scripture

Rom 11:17 — "And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;"

Rom 11:19 — "Thou wilt say then, The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in."

Rom 11:23 — "And they also, if they abide not still in unbelief, shall be graffed in: for God is able to graff them in again."

Rom 11:24 — "For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?"

Modern Corruption

A live corruption on two sides: the Gentile boast that the church simply displaced Israel, and the dispensational cutting of one olive tree into two.

expand to see more

Paul anticipated the corruption and forbade it in advance. The Gentile says, “The branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in” (Rom 11:19) — true enough as a fact, and deadly as a boast. So the apostle answers, Boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. Wherever the church has read her ingrafting as a warrant to despise the natural branches, wherever a supersessionist triumph has hardened into contempt for the Jew, she has spoken the very sentence Romans 11 puts in the mouth of the highminded and rebukes. The wild olive contributed nothing to the tree but its wildness. Grace graffed it in; grace can break it off; and the branch that boasts against the root has forgotten which end of the graft is alive.

The opposite error cuts one tree into two. Dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty of Darby and Scofield, unknown to any Reformation confession — keeps Israel and the church as two peoples with two destinies, which is precisely the arithmetic Paul’s figure forbids. There is one olive tree, one root, one fatness. The natural branches were broken off by unbelief, not by nationality, and “God is able to graff them in again” by the same faith that graffed the Gentile. This is the discipline of the metaphor: no branch stands by descent, and no branch stands by merit. Israel fell by unbelief; the Gentile stands by faith; both stand or fall in one tree, and the husbandman is God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to insert a shoot into another stock, that it may live by a root not its own.

expand to see more

Graff — the older English form of graft.

From Old French grafe, Latin graphium, Greek graphion, “a stylus.”

So called because the cut scion is shaped like a pointed pen.

The wild olive branch is graffed in and partakes of the root (Rom 11:17).

The grafting is contrary to nature, being the work of grace (Rom 11:24).

Usage

"Thou bearest not the root, but the root thee — the graffed branch owes all to the stock."

"Contrary to nature: grace graffs the wild and worthless shoot into the good olive tree."

"God is able to graff them in again — one tree, one root, and every branch there by faith."
